notes.meaning: God's law from Moses was read aloud to the people. This probably happened after Nehemiah came back from Persia, not on the day the wall was dedicated. The passage was Deuteronomy 23:3-5. It said Ammonites and Moabites must not join Israel or marry into it, because long ago they refused Israel food and water and paid Balaam to curse them. God turned that curse into a blessing instead.

The people obeyed right away. They separated from the foreign people they had become tied to, especially through marriages the law did not allow. Matthew Henry notes how hearing God's word read shows us our sin and leads us to turn from it. The word for the mixed group is the same one used for the outsiders who left Egypt with Israel, so the point is about faith and worship, not race.

Eliashib was the high priest, the chief priest over the temple. He was related to Tobiah, an Ammonite and a bitter enemy of God's people. Eliashib turned several temple storerooms into one big room for Tobiah to stay in when he visited. Those rooms had held the tithes (a tenth of the harvest given to God) that fed the Levites, the temple helpers. Matthew Henry calls this almost like setting up an idol in God's house.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Haydock notes the Hebrew could mean either Eliashib or Tobiah set up the room. One older writer says Tobiah rented the rooms and even managed the priests' income.

notes.meaning: All this happened while Nehemiah was away. After about twelve years as governor, he went back to the Persian king, here called king of Babylon because Persia had conquered Babylon. Later he got permission to return and found what Eliashib had done. The Geneva Notes and Matthew Henry say people can slide quickly when a godly leader is gone, like Israel making the golden calf while Moses was on the mountain.

Nehemiah was deeply upset and threw all of Tobiah's things out of the room. Commentators compare this to Jesus clearing the temple. He then had the rooms made clean again by the proper ritual and put the temple supplies back. Matthew Henry draws a lesson for us: to drive sin out of our hearts, we must throw out everything that feeds it, then let Christ fill our hearts with good.

The Levites and singers had not been given their share of food. So they had gone home to farm their own fields to survive, and temple worship stopped. Perhaps the high priest misused the gifts, or the people stopped giving because they saw them being wasted. Matthew Henry says that when God's workers are neglected, God's work gets neglected too.

Nehemiah put the blame on the leaders, who should have prevented this. His question, "Why has the house of God been neglected?", echoes the people's own promise in 10:39 never to neglect it. Then he called the Levites back and put them at their posts again.

Once the Levites were back at work, the people brought in their tithes again. They could see their gifts would now be used rightly. Nehemiah chose honest men from different groups, a priest, a scribe and a Levite, to look after the storerooms and share the supplies fairly. Matthew Henry notes that people should be proven trustworthy before they are given a big trust.

Nehemiah turns to God in a short prayer. He is not boasting or saying God owes him. He asks God to "remember" him, not to reward him. "Do not blot out" is a picture of wiping writing off a scroll. He is simply asking God to look kindly on his honest efforts for God's house.

The Sabbath was Israel's weekly day of rest, set apart for God. Nehemiah saw people pressing grapes, hauling harvest loads and selling food on that day. God's law had said to rest even at harvest time. Traders from Tyre were also selling fish and goods in Jerusalem, and the people of Judah were buying. Nehemiah warned them to stop.

differ.view: The passage upholds the Fourth Commandment, and Christians should keep the Lord's Day holy, with leaders helping protect it.
Christians are not under Israel's strict Sabbath laws, but the passage still teaches us to put God before making money.

notes.meaning: Nehemiah confronted the nobles, the leading men. They were guilty because they allowed it and set a poor example. He reminded them that breaking the Sabbath was one of the sins that brought the earlier disaster and exile, as Jeremiah had warned. Doing it again would only bring more of God's anger.

The Sabbath ran from sunset to sunset. So Nehemiah had the city gates shut as darkness fell before the Sabbath and kept them shut until it was over. He put his own servants on guard, because he could not trust the usual gatekeepers. That way no goods could be brought in for sale.

Traders camped outside the wall once or twice, hoping people would come out to buy. Nehemiah warned them that if they did it again he would use force against them. After that they stopped coming on the Sabbath. Matthew Henry notes that bold, firm action can break bad habits more easily than we might think.

Nehemiah had the Levites make themselves ceremonially clean and guard the gates, so the Sabbath would be kept holy even after he left. Then he prayed again, this time asking God to spare him because of God's great mercy. This shows he did not trust his good works to save him but trusted God's mercy. Matthew Henry thinks the reform lasted, since by Jesus' time the Jews were very strict about the Sabbath.

Nehemiah found Jewish men married to women from Ashdod (a Philistine city), Ammon and Moab. Many of their children spoke their mothers' languages and could not speak the Jews' language. That meant they could not understand God's word in Hebrew. Matthew Henry draws a lesson: children often follow the ungodly parent, so believers should not marry unbelievers, and parents should guard what their children learn to say.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars see this as reflecting a growing sense of ethnic identity after the exile. They note that many other parts of the Hebrew Bible do not object to intermarriage this strongly.

notes.meaning: Nehemiah argued with them and declared God's judgment on them, likely putting them out of the community. Some of the worst offenders were beaten, probably by officers under the law, and had their hair pulled or shaved as a public shame. He made them swear before God not to make such marriages again. Ezra had once pulled out his own hair in sorrow; Nehemiah's anger fell on the wrongdoers.

Nehemiah pointed to King Solomon. He was wise, great and loved by God, yet his foreign wives led him into sin. If Solomon could not stand against this, no one should think they are safe. The problem was marrying people who worshipped other gods, not people of another race, which is why Ruth was welcomed after she turned to Israel's God.

Even the high priest's grandson had married the daughter of Sanballat, a fierce enemy of the Jews. He would not give her up, so Nehemiah drove him away and removed him from the priesthood. The Jewish historian Josephus says this man was Manasseh, who went on to lead a rival temple on Mount Gerizim. That began the long split with the Samaritans seen in John 4.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Haydock notes that if Josephus's dates were right, Sanballat would have been about 150 years old. So some think there were two men named Sanballat.

notes.meaning: Nehemiah asks God to deal with those who had stained the priesthood. Priests were meant to be holy to the Lord, and the high priest was to marry within his own people. Many read this as a prayer for God to hold them to account. Matthew Henry adds that it may also be a prayer for God to bring them to their senses.

Nehemiah sums up his work. He cleared out foreign practices, set each priest and Levite to his task, and arranged for wood for the altar and for the firstfruits (the first part of the harvest given to God). His closing prayer, "Remember me with favor," means "have mercy on me." The people had broken the same promises they made in chapter 10, a reminder that only God's grace, not vows, can truly stop sin.
